claims.claim: New England pond ice was exported by sea to Calcutta, beginning with Frederic Tudor's 1833 shipment aboard the Tuscany.
claims.episode_span: a block of ice cut from a New England pond could travel three months in sawdust, cross the equator, and still be sold in Calcutta
claims.supporting_quote: The first and most profitable of these new routes was to India: in 1833 Tudor combined with the businessmen Samuel Austin and William Rogers to attempt to export ice to Calcutta using the brigantine ship the Tuscany

claims.claim: Shipped ice was packed tightly in sawdust (or hay) as insulation for transport.
claims.episode_span: then used horse-drawn plows and long saws to carve rectangular blocks that were floated to shore, packed in thick layers of sawdust or hay, and stored in heavily insulated ice houses
claims.supporting_quote: The ice was typically packed up tightly with sawdust, and the hold was then closed to prevent warmer air entering; other forms of protective dunnage used to protect ice included hay and pine tree cuttings.

claims.claim: Ice harvesting used horse-drawn cutters that carved uniform rectangular blocks (Nathaniel Wyeth's 1825 invention).
claims.episode_span: Crews waited for lakes to freeze thick enough, then used horse-drawn plows and long saws to carve rectangular blocks
claims.supporting_quote: form of horse-pulled ice-cutter in 1825 that cut square blocks of ice more efficiently than previous methods

claims.claim: In 1805 the American inventor Oliver Evans described a closed vapor-compression refrigeration cycle, though he never built one.
claims.episode_span: Early experimenters such as Oliver Evans and Jacob Perkins sketched closed cycles using volatile liquids
claims.supporting_quote: In 1805, the American inventor Oliver Evans described a closed vapor-compression refrigeration cycle for the production of ice by ether under vacuum.

claims.claim: In 1834 Jacob Perkins built the world's first working vapor-compression refrigeration system.
claims.episode_span: by the 1830s working vapor-compression machines existed that could freeze water in modest quantities
claims.supporting_quote: In 1834, an American expatriate to Great Britain, Jacob Perkins , built the first working vapor-compression refrigeration system in the world.

claims.claim: Mechanical/plant refrigeration displaced the natural ice trade in the early twentieth century, with domestic refrigerators common in US homes by the 1930s.
claims.episode_span: By the early twentieth century mechanical refrigeration had displaced the ice trade for most urban and industrial uses
claims.supporting_quote: In the years after the war, the natural ice industry collapsed into insignificance

claims.claim: Early refrigerants such as ammonia and sulfur dioxide were hazardous toxic gases.
claims.episode_span: ammonia is toxic, sulfur dioxide is corrosive, and the later chlorofluorocarbons proved destructive to the ozone layer
claims.supporting_quote: Prior to, and during the 1920s, refrigerators used toxic gases as refrigerants, including ammonia, sulphur dioxide, and chloromethane.

claims.claim: CFC refrigerants contributed to ozone depletion and were phased out under the Montreal Protocol.
claims.episode_span: the later chlorofluorocarbons proved destructive to the ozone layer
claims.supporting_quote: As a result of CFCs contributing to ozone depletion in the upper atmosphere , the manufacture of such compounds has been phased out under the Montreal Protocol , and they are being replaced with other products such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)

claims.claim: The brig Tuscany left Boston for Calcutta on 12 May 1833 with 180 tons of ice and arrived in September with 100 tons remaining, i.e. roughly 45% lost to melting in transit.
claims.episode_span: A large share of the original mass could disappear to melting in transit and storage; what survived still commanded high prices because no alternative existed.
claims.supporting_quote: On May 12, 1833, the brig Tuscany sailed from Boston for Calcutta, its hold filled with 180 tons of ice cut during the winter. When it approached the Ganges in September 1833, many believed the delivery was an elaborate joke, but the ship still had 100 tons of ice upon arrival.

claims.claim: Carl von Linde's 1876 compressed-ammonia refrigerator made ammonia, sulfur dioxide and methyl chloride the standard refrigerants until the late 1920s despite safety concerns; Frigidaire's first self-contained unit (1923) and Freon expanded the household market in the 1930s.
claims.episode_span: Early refrigerants introduced new problems—ammonia is toxic, sulfur dioxide is corrosive, and the later chlorofluorocarbons proved destructive to the ozone layer
claims.supporting_quote: His new process made possible the use of gases such as ammonia (NH 3 ), sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) and methyl chloride (CH 3 Cl) as refrigerants, which were widely used for that purpose until the late 1920s despite safety concerns.

claims.claim: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was signed in 1987, and its later amendments targeted a complete phaseout of CFCs in developed countries by 1996.
claims.episode_span: the later chlorofluorocarbons proved destructive to the ozone layer—so the industry had to iterate again on fluid chemistry without losing the thermodynamic advantages already achieved
claims.source_title: International Treaties and Cooperation about the Protection of the Stratospheric Ozone Layer | US EPA
claims.supporting_quote: This cooperation resulted in the signing of the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer in 1987. After the Montreal Protocol was signed, new data showed worse-than-expected damage to the ozone layer. In 1992, the Parties to the Protocol decided to alter the terms of the 1987 agreement to end production of halons by 1994 and CFCs by 1996 in developed countries.
